verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster. Of David. A psalm.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster. David's, a psalm to be sung.
verses.directors_commentary: The three words are a stage direction, not part of the poem. In the Hebrew text this line is verse 1; the KJV prints it as a heading and starts counting at the next line, which is why every number in this psalm differs by one between Bible versions. 'Choirmaster' (lamnatzeach) names the one who directs the music, and 'mizmor' is a song sung with instrumental accompaniment. 'Of David' (ledavid) can mean by him, for him or about him, so do not play it as a signature but as a dedication. The commentators agree that the psalm was spoken after a rescue: Radak and Meiri say after recovery from sickness, and Malbim after a miraculous escape from enemies, with a thanksgiving offering brought. The KJV 'chief Musician' is a fair rendering of the title.

philological_notes.note: A participle with the preposition 'to', conventionally 'to the choirmaster' or 'to the leader'. The root nitzeach carries the sense of pre-eminence or lasting, which suits one who leads. The Targum does not translate it as a person but as a purpose: lishabbacha, 'for praising'.
A song with instrumental accompaniment, from zamar to make music. The Targum renders it 'praise' (tushbachta).

verses.translation_literal: Waiting, I waited for YHWH, and he stretched out to me and he heard my cry for help.
verses.translation_dramatic: I waited. I waited for the LORD, and the waiting was all I had. Then he bent down toward me and he heard, he heard the cry I could not hold back.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice is that of a man who has finished waiting and now says what the waiting was like. The opening doubles the same verb, 'waiting I waited', an emphatic form that the KJV softens into 'patiently' and the YLT into 'diligently'. The Hebrew does not say patiently; it says the whole man was stretched toward God, and only the length of the waiting is stressed. Play the repetition, do not decorate it. 'He stretched out to me' has no object: the sentence says that he leaned, and Rashi supplies 'his ear', Radak 'he came near to me', and Ibn Ezra stresses that God dwells on high, so the stooping is a descent. The KJV 'inclined unto me' is fair. 'Cry for help' (shav'ah) is not polite prayer; it is the shout of someone in danger, the same word used for the Israelites in Egypt in Exod 2:23.

philological_notes.note: An infinitive absolute before a finite verb of the same root, which adds emphasis: 'I really waited' or 'I kept on waiting'. Ibn Ezra says qavveh is an unusual form for the infinitive absolute, parallel to Ps 118:18, yasor yissarani Yah.
'He stretched out to me', literally 'bent toward me', with no stated object. Rashi supplies 'his ear'; Radak explains it as nearness, citing Ps 145:18.

verses.translation_literal: And he brought me up from a pit of roaring, from mud of mire, and he set my feet upon a rock, he established my steps.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he drew me up out of the pit where the waters roared, out of the thick mud of the mire. He set my feet upon a rock, and he made every step I took stand firm.
verses.directors_commentary: The pit is a cistern or a flooded hole, the kind of place where a man could stand in wet clay up to his thighs and sink as he struggled. The picture is a rescue, but the commentators disagree on what from: Rashi hears the prisoners of Egypt and the roaring of the sea, while Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as a metaphor for sickness or distress, Radak saying that a sick man fears death as one who falls in a pit fears drowning. The Hebrew is more physical than the translations. The KJV 'horrible pit' follows an old reading of sha'on as 'desolation'; Ibn Ezra rejects this, and the word elsewhere means the roar of water or crowds (Isa 17:12), so a 'pit of roaring' is a pit with water noise. 'Miry clay' puts one noun after another: tit hayaven, mud of mire, two near-synonyms stacked to sound like sucking mud. The movement of the verse is up (he brought up, he set up) and then the rock: the rock opposes the pit, as Ibn Ezra says. 'Established my steps' is literally that the footfalls are made firm, so the new problem is not only standing but walking.

philological_notes.note: A pit of roaring: sha'on is the din of waters, crowds or armies. Ibn Ezra says the right reading is 'noise of many waters', rejecting the derivation from sho'ah, desolation, that stands behind the KJV 'horrible'. Malbim has 'filled with roaring, surging water'.

Mud of mire: yaven is the sticky silt at the bottom of water, found again in Ps 69:3 'I sink in the mire of the deep' (Metzudat Zion). Radak compares the construct to 'dust of earth' (Dan 12:2), two nouns for one substance.
'My steps'; KJV 'goings'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion gloss it as my feet or steps.

verses.translation_literal: And he put in my mouth a new song, praise to our God. Many will see and they will fear, and they will trust in YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see it, and they will be afraid, and they will learn to trust in the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker does not say 'I made a song'; he says that God put it in his mouth. The song is a gift, the way breath is. Rashi connects it with the Song of the Sea (Exod 15), and Radak says that a person must make a new song for each new miracle. Malbim adds the logic: a rescue by natural means earns an old song, one by a miracle earns a new one. 'Our God' widens the circle in the middle of the verse, and Ibn Ezra notes that this plural is for the sake of those many who will see. Then the three verbs follow in a chain: they see, they fear, they trust, which turns private thanksgiving into public witness. The 'fear' here is awe, as in 'fear of YHWH', not terror, and the KJV 'shall see it, and fear' adds 'it' where the Hebrew leaves the object open. The verbs after 'see' are imperfect and may express purpose: they see so that they fear and trust.

philological_notes.note: A new song. The phrase marks a response to a fresh act of God (Ps 33:3, 96:1, 98:1). Rashi identifies it with the Song of the Sea; Radak says one must renew praise for each miracle.
A play on sound: yir'u 'they will see' and yira'u 'they will fear' are written with the same consonants apart from the doubled yod. The ear hears seeing turn into fear.

verses.translation_literal: Blessednesses of the man who has made YHWH his trust, and has not turned to the arrogant, and those who swerve to falsehood.
verses.translation_dramatic: Oh, the happiness of the man who has made the LORD his trust, who did not turn toward the proud, nor to those who stray after lies.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Ashrei' is a cry, not a sentence: literally 'oh, the happinesses of', a plural of intensity. The KJV 'blessed' makes it a religious label, but the word is closer to 'how fortunate!', and it is what a crowd says when it sees a man who has come through. The man is a gever, an able-bodied man who is expected to look to someone for help, and the verse says to whom people usually turned: the rehavim, the arrogant or the powerful, and those who 'swerve' (sotei) toward falsehood. Rashi and Radak say the rehavim are the proud or the strong; Ibn Ezra reads them as people of strength to whom one runs for help. The KJV 'respecteth not' is a free rendering of 'did not turn to', which is a physical motion, as one turns one's face to a patron. Malbim adds a distinction that a man may trust God and still have another thing as his real trust; this man made YHWH himself his trust. The word rahav also names a sea monster elsewhere in the psalms (Ps 89:11, Isa 51:9), and an ancient listener may have heard that echo, but that is my own reading.

philological_notes.note: Arrogant, bold or overbearing people; Rashi connects it with the verb in Isa 3:5 'the youth will be insolent toward the elder'. Radak says it is an adjective in the pattern of 'reshaim'.

Those who swerve or veer off toward falsehood. Rashi says they stray from the straight path after the lie; Radak and Meiri say the root is either shut or shatah (as in Num 5:12, 'if his wife goes astray') and the meaning is one. Metzudat Zion compares Prov 7:25.

verses.translation_literal: Many things you have done, you, YHWH my God, your wonders and your plans toward us; there is no arranging to you. I would declare and I would speak: they are too many to recount.
verses.translation_dramatic: How many things you have done, LORD, my God: your wonders, and the plans you laid for us. There is no one to set beside you. I would tell them, I would speak them out, but they are too many to count.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker turns from the crowd to God, and the grammar changes with him: from 'he' to 'you'. The verse has two big words side by side: 'wonders' (niflaot), what he does, and 'plans' (machshavot), what he intended before he acted. Radak says the wonders are the acts and the plans come before them, and notes that the Torah speaks in human language when it gives God thoughts; Meiri says the plans are the care with which God arranges rescue. 'Toward us' (eleinu) is awkward, and Ibn Ezra lists both 'for our sake' and 'as it says'. The hardest phrase is 'ein arokh eleikha'. The verb arakh is 'to set in order, to line up, to compare', so it can mean 'no one can be matched with you' (Rashi, Metzudat David) or 'they cannot be arranged in order before you' (KJV). Both readings are held by the commentators, and the Hebrew allows both. The KJV 'cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee' follows the second reading; the literal layer keeps 'arranging', which carries both senses. The last clause is the grammar of a man who begins and gives up: 'I would declare and I would speak', and then 'they are too many'.

philological_notes.note: Arakh means to arrange, set in a row, or to value and compare. Rashi: no ruler or saviour can be compared to you, citing 'according to your valuation' (Lev 27:12). Radak gives two ways: no one can set out in order the wonders before you, or none can be compared to you, as in Ps 86:8 and 89:7. Ibn Ezra: no human can arrange them for you.

Your plans or intentions. Radak says the 'wonders' are the work at the time of doing and the 'plans' are the thought beforehand, a human way of speaking, and compares Jer 18:11. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'your decrees'.

verses.translation_literal: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; ears you dug for me. Burnt offering and sin offering you did not ask.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sacrifice and gift-offering were not what you wanted. What you gave me was ears, hollowed out for hearing. Burnt offering and sin offering, you never asked.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the most startling line of the psalm, and the temple singer says it with calm. It names four of the main kinds of offering, the whole shared meal (zevach), the grain gift (minchah), the whole-burnt offering (olah) and the offering for wrongdoing (chatta'ah), and says that none were what God wanted. In the ancient world, where sacrifice was the language of every relationship with a god, this is a sharp turn. The commentators do not read it as an abolition: Radak argues that God's first command was to listen, and the offerings came after sin, and quotes 1 Sam 15:22, 'to obey is better than sacrifice'; Ibn Ezra reads 'you did not ask for sacrifice, but dug ears for me to hear your voice'. The key word is the verb kara, 'dig', as in digging a pit or a well (Exod 21:33). The KJV 'opened' softens it into a gentle word; the Hebrew has a spade in it. God dug out the ears, as one digs a channel, so that sound could enter. Rashi says 'made them hollow to hear', and Metzudat Zion 'dug'. (The Greek of Hebrews 10:5 reads 'a body you prepared', a different tradition; the Hebrew has ears.) 'Did not ask for' (lo sha'alta) is the language of a request, which is more modest than a command: God did not demand them.

philological_notes.note: 'You dug ears for me.' Kara is the verb for digging a pit or a well (Exod 21:33), cited by Radak and Metzudat Zion; Rashi says 'you made them hollow to hear'. 'Opened' (KJV) is an interpretation, 'prepared' (YLT) another. The dual 'ears' is a natural dual for a paired organ.
The whole-burnt offering, which rises entirely on the altar, and the sin offering. Radak says the olah atones for neglected positive commands and the chata'ah is the sin offering of Lev 4.

verses.translation_literal: Then I said, Here, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written on me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then I said, Here I am. I have come. In the scroll of the book, it is written about me.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Then' (az) is the hinge: because ears were dug, the answer is to come. 'Hineh', here, is a word of presenting oneself, the word of someone who answers a summons, as Abraham and Samuel say 'hineni'. The scene of the speaker walking to the front with a scroll in mind is the point of the verse. But which scroll? 'Megillat sefer' is literally 'scroll of a book', both words meaning something written; the KJV 'volume of the book' is a fair guess. The commentators divide. Rashi and Metzudat David say it is the moment at Sinai, 'we will do and we will hear' (Exod 24:7), and the book is the Torah of Moses. Ibn Ezra offers a second: David had vowed in distress to sing a new song, and now arrives to fulfil it. Malbim takes it as the law written inside a man. 'Written on me' (alay) may mean 'written about me', 'upon me as an obligation', or 'for me'. The KJV 'of me' picks the first. A director should not decide for the actor which one it is; the actor can play a man who found his duty in writing and now meets it with his body.

philological_notes.note: A scroll of a book, from the root gll 'to roll'. Metzudat Zion compares it with 'a flying scroll' (Zech 5:1) and says it means a letter or document; Radak, Rashi and Meiri identify it with the Torah.
Written 'on me': the preposition al can mean about, concerning, upon, or incumbent on. Radak: written about me and about every one of your people.

verses.translation_literal: To do your will, my God, I have desired, and your torah is in the midst of my inward parts.
verses.translation_dramatic: To do your will, my God, is what I wanted. And your teaching lies deep inside me, in the very centre of my body.
verses.directors_commentary: The man who has said that God did not want sacrifices now says what God does want, and what he himself wants: the same verb, chafatz, appears here and in the previous verse. In v. 7 God did not 'desire' offerings, and here the speaker 'desires' to do his will. The two desires meet. The second half is bodily: 'torah' is the teaching or instruction, not only the written law, and it is placed 'in the midst of my me'ai', the intestines, bowels or inner organs. The KJV 'within my heart' replaces a gut with a heart. Radak says the heart is included in the me'im, and Metzudat David says the law is kept in the heart that is one of the inner parts; Rashi reads it in the daily act of eating, saying that even his food is eaten according to your torah. Ibn Ezra adds 'in secret', recalling Ezekiel's eating of the scroll. The picture is of law swallowed, digested, made part of the body: an ancient listener, who thought of the bowels as the seat of feeling and conscience, would hear that the law is not on a shelf.

philological_notes.note: The inward parts, bowels or belly; the organs where compassion and anguish are felt. Radak says it means 'my heart', since the heart is among the inward parts, and stresses that the thought does not leave. Rashi says the law governs even his meals. KJV 'heart' replaces the bodily word.
'I have desired, I have delighted.' The same verb as in v. 7: God did not desire sacrifice, but I desire to do your will.

verses.translation_literal: I have borne glad news of righteousness in the great assembly. Here, my lips I do not restrain; YHWH, you know.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have carried the good news of justice into the great assembly. Look, I do not hold my lips shut. LORD, you know it.
verses.directors_commentary: The scene moves from the heart to the public square. The 'great assembly' (qahal rav) is the gathered people, a national gathering for a festival or a thanksgiving at the Temple, where such a speaker would stand. The verb bissarti is from the root of 'glad news' (besorah): the KJV 'preached' gives it a pulpit, but the word is that of a messenger who runs with news. Radak points out that the same root can carry bad news (1 Sam 4:17), so the verb itself is neutral; the message here is good. What he brings is 'tzedek', righteousness, and the Hebrew gives it no suffix, so the actor must choose whose it is. Read with the next verse, where it is 'your righteousness', it is God's saving justice, and that is the reading the dramatic layer follows. Malbim takes it as the speaker's own righteousness (tzidki), and hears an anxiety that the man will seem to boast, which he answers with 'YHWH, you know' that his motive is not self-praise. Either way the closing line is the same: 'lo ekhla', 'I do not restrain', uses the verb of the flood being 'restrained' in Gen 8:2 (Rashi), a dam held back, and here no dam holds. 'YHWH, you know' is a short, firm line: say it quietly, because only God can see whether the speaker is telling the truth.

philological_notes.note: To bring news, usually good news. Ibn Ezra and Radak say the root can mean any news, good or bad, as in 'the messenger answered' (1 Sam 4:17); here, good. The KJV 'preached' is an interpretive word, not a literal one.
'Righteousness', here without a suffix. It may be God's, as in the parallel 'your righteousness' of v. 11, or the speaker's own, as Malbim reads it ('that is, my righteousness').
'I do not restrain.' Rashi: 'I do not hold back', the verb of Gen 8:2, where the rain was restrained. Metzudat Zion gives the same. The same root returns in v. 12 'you will not withhold'.

verses.translation_literal: Your righteousness I have not covered in the midst of my heart; your faithfulness and your salvation I have spoken; I have not hidden your covenant loyalty and your truth to the great assembly.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your justice I have not buried inside my heart. Your faithfulness and your rescue, I spoke them. I have not hidden your steadfast love and your truth from the great assembly.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built as a mirror: two things are not concealed, two things are spoken, and two more are not hidden, so that the line says the same thing three times with different pairs of words. The first and third halves are negative ('not covered', 'not hidden') and the middle is positive ('I have spoken'). The words are the stock of the covenant: tzidkah (righteousness, God's saving justice), emunah (faithfulness), teshuah (salvation), chesed (covenant loyalty, which the KJV renders 'lovingkindness', a word Coverdale made) and emet (truth, in the sense of reliability). Radak distinguishes the last pair: emet is the keeping of a promise, chesed is what goes beyond it. The last words say 'to the great assembly' (le-qahal rav), not 'from'. English 'hide from' reverses the direction, which is why the KJV and most versions write 'from the congregation'. Radak and Meiri argue that the phrase belongs with 'I have spoken', since a verb of hiding would otherwise take 'from' (min). The literal layer keeps the Hebrew 'to' so that the question stays open; the dramatic layer takes the usual English sense. Speak the line so that both are heard. The picture of 'covering' something 'in the midst of the heart' is of a coal buried under ash, which the speaker refuses to do.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty and truth, a fixed pair that recurs in the psalms. Radak: emet is carrying out the promised good, chesed is the surplus beyond what was promised. Malbim in v. 10 separates chesed (done without prior merit or promise) from emet (done on account of a merit or promise).
Literally 'to the great assembly'. Radak and Meiri say this phrase belongs with 'I have spoken', not with 'I have not hidden', because the latter would take 'from' (min), as in Josh 7:19.

verses.translation_literal: You, YHWH, will not withhold your compassion from me; your covenant loyalty and your truth continually will guard me.
verses.translation_dramatic: And you, LORD, do not shut away your compassion from me. Let your steadfast love and your truth stand guard over me, always.
verses.directors_commentary: The first half of the psalm is thanksgiving; here, with the little word 'you' placed first for emphasis, it turns toward the future, and the speaker asks for what he has already received. 'Rachamim' is compassion, and it comes from the word for the womb (rechem), the love of a mother for what she bore: the KJV 'tender mercies' is nearer to this than the modern 'mercy'. The verb 'withhold' (kala) is the same word as 'restrain' in v. 10: the speaker did not restrain his lips, and he asks that God not restrain his compassion. This is a deliberate echo: a man who has given everything away asks that he not be shut out. 'Chesed and emet' return from v. 11 as two guards, 'they will guard me' (yitzeruni), a verb used of a watchman or of a city under guard. The Hebrew form can be read as a plea (KJV, ASV, Webster: 'withhold not', 'let them preserve') or as a confident statement (YLT). Radak and Meiri hear a plea that the same help continue, and Metzudat David a claim: because I told of you, you will not withhold. The actor can hold both: a plea spoken with the voice of someone who expects to be answered. The word 'continually' (tamid) is the same as in the daily offering (olat tamid): the daily sacrifice that the speaker has just said God did not ask for is replaced by a daily guarding.

philological_notes.note: Compassion, from rechem 'womb': the tenderness one has for what one has borne. The plural is of intensity. Rashi glosses lo tikhla as 'you will not withhold'.
'They guard me', with doubled tzade from the root ntzr. Rashi: 'they will keep me'. Ibn Ezra: the chesed and emet that I told to the assembly will themselves guard me from every foe.

verses.translation_literal: For evils have surrounded upon me until there is no number; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I was not able to see; they are numerous more than the hairs of my head, and my heart has abandoned me.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have closed around me, the evils, ring on ring on ring, more than any hand could count. My own guilt has run me down, and I cannot lift my eyes to look it in the face. Thicker than the hairs of my head they lie on me, and my heart, my very heart, has slipped away and left me standing here alone.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has just praised God before the great assembly; now the voice drops and the confession begins. Play it as a man who has run out of breath, not as theatre. In the ancient Israelite view misfortune and guilt travel together: trouble is what iniquity looks like when it arrives. That is why 'evils' (ra'ot) and 'iniquities' ('avonot) sit side by side, and why Radak, citing the Talmud, says a person should fear that sin may cause hardship. The word 'avon can mean both the guilt and its punishment, which Ibn Ezra stresses, so 'my iniquities have overtaken me' is not only a sorry list but a pursuit, with guilt as the pursuer who has caught him.

The KJV 'compassed me about' is accurate but archaic; 'afefu is 'surrounded', and Radak glosses it with the same verb as 'the waves of death surrounded me' (2 Sam 22:5). The KJV 'I am not able to look up' adds a direction the Hebrew lacks: the verb is plain 'to see', and BBE's 'bent down with their weight' goes further still. Is he too ashamed to look, too blinded by tears, too overwhelmed to take it in? Hebrew allows each, and the medieval commentators split between them. The hairs of the head, in the ancient world, were a proverbial number past counting, and 'my heart has abandoned me' means courage and mind both: in Hebrew thought the heart is the seat of thinking, so he is saying he has lost his nerve and his wits together. The KJV 'faileth me' softens a verb that is bluntly 'abandoned'.

philological_notes.note: 'Surrounded', as an army or flood surrounds. The same verb opens the lament over death's waves in 2 Sam 22:5 and Ps 18:5 (18:4 in English), where the 'cords of death' surround the singer; the evils here close in with that same weight.
'My iniquities': 'avon covers the wrongdoing and the consequence it brings, so the word can name the guilt and the punishment in a single breath.
'And my heart has abandoned me': the heart is the seat of mind and will, so this is the collapse of courage and of judgment together.

verses.translation_literal: Be pleased, YHWH, to deliver me; YHWH, to my help, make haste.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be willing, LORD. Be willing to pull me out. LORD, to my help, hurry.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the long weight of the last verse, the lines shrink to a few words, and the speed must show in the speaking: two short phrases, the divine name said twice, and a final single word that is a command. Play it as a whisper that cannot wait. 'Be pleased' (retzeh) is the language of favor and willingness, not a polite request: he asks God to want this, as Radak puts it, 'let it be your will'. The Metzudat David adds that once God is willing, no one can hold back his hand.

The KJV 'make haste to help me' puts the helping in the verb and loses the Hebrew order. The Hebrew sets 'to my help' (le'ezrati) before the imperative chushah, so the plea arrives help first and haste last, with the closing word landing like a shove. The KJV also turns the second 'YHWH' into a stray 'O Lord' in the middle of the clause, but the Hebrew repeats the name as a second cry. Almost the same lines recur at the opening of Psalm 70, a sign the plea was used on its own as a short prayer.

philological_notes.note: 'Be pleased', 'be willing': an imperative of favor, asking God to will the rescue rather than merely to carry it out.
'To my help'. Ibn Ezra offers two readings: 'to be my help', or an adjective-like form, like le'ezreni ('to help me').
'Hurry!' An imperative of the root meaning to hasten, with a final -ah that lends urgency; it stands last in the verse, as the climax of the plea.

verses.translation_literal: May they be ashamed and abashed together, the seekers of my life to sweep it away; may they be turned back backward and humiliated, the delighters in my evil.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them blush, let them wither, all of them together, those who hunt my life to sweep it off the earth. Let them be driven back, back the way they came, and burn with disgrace, every one who takes delight in my ruin.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns from plea to curse, but a curse in a public voice: it asks that the enemies' plans fail in the open, in front of everyone. In the ancient Near East shame was the public loss of standing, the opposite of the honor a man's family and name rested on, and a hunter driven off empty-handed was shamed in front of the whole village. So the wish is not for blood. It is that the pursuers be seen to lose. Metzudat David reads 'they will be ashamed' as what happens when they see the speaker rescued.

The KJV 'seek after my soul' hides the Hebrew nefesh, which is also 'life' and 'throat': these men want his life, not his spiritual state. The verb lispotah, 'to sweep away', is stronger than the KJV's 'destroy'; Rashi glosses it 'to finish it', pointing to the Aramaic of Deut 2:14, 'until the whole generation was finished'. Radak and Ibn Ezra tie it to Abraham's 'Will you sweep away (tispeh) the righteous with the wicked?' (Gen 18:23). The verse also closes with a pun on the previous one: the 'evils' (ra'ot) that surrounded him in v. 13 now return as the 'evil' (ra'ati) these men want for him, the ASV 'delight in my hurt' and KJV 'wish me evil' both being fair. The phrase 'turned back backward' repeats the sense of retreat on purpose, as a soldier turns and runs.

philological_notes.note: 'To sweep it away', 'to finish it off'. Rashi glosses it as 'to finish it', following the Targum of Deut 2:14 ('ad desaf kol dara', until the whole generation was finished). Radak and Ibn Ezra compare Gen 18:23 'ha'af tispeh'. Metzudat Zion also compares Jeremiah's 'the beasts are swept away'.
'May they be turned back backward': the verb already means turning back, and 'achor adds the direction. Metzudat David pictures a man ashamed who retreats on his heels.

'Those who delight in my evil': chafetz is delight or wanting, so these are not only attackers but people who enjoy the thought of his harm. Malbim distinguishes them from the 'seekers of my life' as hidden haters who only desire his hurt.

verses.translation_literal: May they be appalled on the heel of their shame, those saying to me, "Aha! Aha!"
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be left standing in the silence of their own disgrace, appalled, on the heels of their shame. They were the ones who said to me, "Aha! Aha!"
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the cruellest verse in the passage because it is the sound of laughter. 'Aha!' (הֶאָח) is not a word, it is a noise: the crow of someone watching another fall. The Hebrew says it twice, and the actors should say it twice, with a grin. The same cry appears in Psalm 35:21 ('Aha, aha, our eye has seen'), as Radak and Malbim note, and Radak glosses it simply 'joy, joy'. These are not enemies in a fight, they are spectators who enjoy it. Rashi hears exactly this: when disaster comes, they praise themselves over my misfortune.

The curse is built on a pun of sound and sense: 'may they be appalled' (יָשֹׁמּוּ) is from the root that gives 'desolation' (שַׁמָּה), and the wished punishment is a silent, stunned emptiness set against their noisy glee. The KJV's 'let them be desolate' keeps the root but pairs it with 'for a reward of their shame', and here the Hebrew word עֵקֶב is double. It is the common word for 'heel', and from 'the heel of' comes 'in consequence of, as the wage for'. Rashi holds to 'heel' and measure-for-measure: shame follows on their heels, by the road they walked against me. Radak, Metzudat David and Meiri take it as 'reward, recompense', as in Deuteronomy 7:12. The KJV's 'reward' takes only the second reading, and the English reader never meets the heel.

The word 'shame' (בֹּשֶׁת) is the Hebrew's strongest social penalty, a loss of standing before the community, and the mockers' own word of 'Aha' is turned back on them as the sentence.

philological_notes.note: 'heel', and by extension 'what follows on the heel': consequence, wage, reward. Rashi reads it as 'heel', in the sense of measure for measure; Radak and Metzudat David read it as 'reward', as in Deuteronomy 7:12. English must choose, but Hebrew holds both.
'aha, aha': an interjection of malicious joy, the crow of a spectator at another's fall. Radak glosses it 'joy' and cites Psalm 35:21.
'may they be appalled, desolated': the root of 'desolation'; the wished fate is stunned silence. Rashi glosses it 'may they be astonished', Metzudat Zion 'desolation'.

verses.translation_literal: May they exult and may they rejoice in you, all those seeking you; may they say continually, "YHWH is great," those loving your salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: But let those who seek you break into joy, and rejoice in you, every one. Let those who love your rescue say it without ceasing: "Great is the LORD!"
verses.directors_commentary:
The sound of the scene turns here. The mockers' short, bitter 'Aha' gives way to long open vowels of gladness: 'exult' and 'rejoice' are two different verbs for joy, set one after the other so the line seems to climb. Radak notes the contrast outright: the enemies are made desolate, but all who seek the LORD are to rejoice.

Two groups mirror the two of verse 15. The enemies 'seek my life'; these 'seek you'. Those who 'delight in my harm' are matched by those who 'love your salvation'. Malbim reads this as a sharp distinction: someone who only wants the result of rescue would rather never have needed it; but those who love salvation itself are glad to need it continually, since each rescue makes the LORD's name greater. That is a richer reading than the KJV's smooth 'such as love thy salvation'.

The quoted cry, 'YHWH is great' (יִגְדַּל יְהוָה), uses an imperfect verb that can be a wish ('may the LORD be magnified') or a plain statement. The KJV and ASV make it a wish, the YLT a statement. In the mouth of a crowd it should sound like both, a shout. Radak says the LORD's name grows greater in the world each time he does miracles for the devout, and everyone says, 'He is great and works wonders.' 'Continually' (תָּמִיד) is the word for the daily standing offering, a rhythm of ritual, not a mood.

philological_notes.note: 'may they exult and may they rejoice': two verbs for joy in a pair, the second the common word for gladness; the first is the rarer, more exultant verb.
'YHWH is great / may YHWH be magnified': an imperfect verb that can be a wish or a statement; Radak says the name grows greater as he does wonders for the devout.
'continually': the word for the daily offering (the tamid), so a rhythm and not only a mood.

verses.translation_literal: And I, poor and needy, may the Lord reckon to me; my help and my deliverer, you; my God, do not delay.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I am poor. I am needy. Let the Lord take account of me. You are my help, you are the one who gets me out. My God, do not be late.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends not on the crowd's praise but on one person alone, with open hands. The sentence order is the whole drama: 'And I, poor and needy', said first, before any verb. Everything the speaker has to offer is in that phrase. 'Poor' (עָנִי) is the man bent low by hardship; 'needy' (אֶבְיוֹן) is the man who wants, who has not enough of anything. Metzudat Zion says the needy is lower than the poor, because he lacks everything. Radak adds that even David, a king, is poor and needy before God. In the ancient world, the poor had no legal power and no patron: the only protector was the god.

The line 'may the Lord reckon to me' (יַחֲשָׁב לִי) has no stated object, and the KJV fills it in with 'yet the Lord thinketh upon me', turning a jussive into a statement of comfort. The BBE does the same ('has me in mind'). The Hebrew verb is imperfect and can be read 'may he count' or 'let him credit'. Rashi gives it as 'give me a heart to think of my poverty'; Radak lists three options, including 'credit my poverty as atonement for iniquities' and 'make me count for something in your eyes'; Metzudat David reads 'credit my humility to me as merit'. The text is difficult and the actors should leave it open.

The verse ends on the same urgency as verse 14: 'do not delay' (אַל־תְּאַחַר). Radak links it back, since 'hurry' was the earlier word. The KJV's 'make no tarrying' is archaic: tarrying is lingering, and a modern reader would hear a stroll. The Hebrew is the flat 'don't be late', and the poor man's fear is the lateness of the one who owes him help. Note 'Lord' here is Adonai, a different word from the YHWH of verses 14 and 17.

philological_notes.note: 'poor and needy': the pair is a stock phrase for those without protection. Metzudat Zion says the needy is lower still, lacking all things.
'may he reckon to me': a hard phrase with no stated object. Readings include 'think of me', 'credit my humility to me', 'count me worthy'.
'do not delay': a negative jussive of the verb for lateness. Ibn Ezra notes that the verb can be intransitive, as in 'why do they tarry'.
